snippets.text: Primary intestinal lymphoma accounts for ∼20% of malignancies of the small bowel. These neoplasms are non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas; they usually have a diffuse, large-cell histology and are of T cell origin. Intestinal lymphoma involves the ileum, jejunum, and duodenum, in decreasing frequency—a pattern that mirrors the relative amount of normal lymphoid cells in these anatomic areas. The risk of small-bowel lymphoma is increased in patients with a prior history of malabsorptive conditions (e.g., celiac sprue), regional enteritis, and depressed immune function due to congenital immunodeficiency syndromes, prior organ transplantation, autoimmune disorders, or AIDS.

snippets.text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between DLBCL and BL (BCL-U) is a category in the 2008 WHO lymphoma classification. The reason WHO made it become one of B-cell lymphoma classification, is because it presents as a high-grade B-cell lymphoma but cannot be more precisely classified since it does not meet the criteria diagnostic for either BL or DLBCL. It seems likely that most of the tumors in this category are the high-grade end of the spectrum of DLBCL.

snippets.text: Definitive management of midgut malrotation is surgical. The Ladd procedure, comprising counterclockwise derotation of any volvulus, division of Ladd’s bands, broadening of the mesenteric base, placement of small bowel on the right and colon on the left, and usually an appendectomy, does not restore normal rotation but aims to eliminate duodenal obstruction and reduce the risk of recurrent volvulus. Outcomes are excellent when diagnosis is timely, and bowel remains viable; however, mortality and long-term morbidity increase substantially in the presence of extensive ischemia, prematurity, severe cardiac disease, or complex syndromic associations.

snippets.text: In adults, malrotation is uncommon and typically presents with chronic, nonspecific symptoms rather than catastrophic volvulus, which occurs in only a minority of cases. Many report long histories of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, bloating, or episodic vomiting, often triggered by meals and sometimes associated with weight loss or food avoidance. A subset presents with acute small-bowel obstruction or midgut volvulus, characterised by sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to initial examination, repeated bilious or feculent vomiting, and rapid hemodynamic deterioration if diagnosis is delayed.

snippets.text: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is a potentially life-threatening disorder of young infants. It is far more common than BS. As in perinatal BS, there is a predisposition for (atypical) presentation in premature infants. Affected infants may present with projectile, nonbilious vomiting and an abdominal mass arising from hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter. Loss of gastric acid results in hypochloremia and secondary hyperaldosteronism produces hypokalemia (Table 2 and Figure 4). Diagnostic urinary chloride is often <20 mEq/L, while the value is >20 mEq/L in BS (Figure 4). Mimicking the presentation of antenatal BS is a rare report of an early-onset IHPS in association with prematurity and polyhydramnios.

snippets.text: As in cases of other causes of gastrointestinal bleeding, a technetium-99M tagged RBC scan is helpful in the diagnosis of acute gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to a Meckel’s diverticulum but does not help diagnose a Meckel’s diverticulum as a cause for the bleed. When triphasic CT angiography is used for the evaluation of acute gastrointestinal bleeding, it may be able to identify active gastrointestinal hemorrhage and Meckel’s diverticulum as a cause of this hemorrhage (Fig. 16). On digital subtraction angiography, active bleeding may be identified in the superior mesenteric artery territory as the blood supply to the Meckel’s diverticulum is by the superior mesenteric artery. A persistent vitelline artery, the source of embryonic supply to Meckel’s diverticulum, if present, can be seen as an elongated vessel arising from the distal ileal artery. A bleeding Meckel’s diverticulum can demonstrate contrast extravasation into the diverticulum and the adjacent small bowel. Occasionally, focal dense capillary contrast stain in a Meckel’s diverticulum can be seen, indicating the presence of ectopic gastric mucosa.

snippets.text: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. There is no clear familial predisposition. Patients with other malformations of the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, or cardiovascular system have an increased risk of having a Meckel diverticulum. The prevalence of Meckel diverticulum in the general population is approximately 2%; however, it is difficult to determine the exact number because many patients are asymptomatic.[1] The patient often becomes symptomatic in the first decade of life with an average age of 2.5.[2]

snippets.text: Meckel’s diverticulitis is a result of obstruction to the neck of the diverticulum that can occur secondary to inflammatory narrowing, stricture formation, or mechanical obstruction due to enteroliths or other less common causes such as food, foreign body, or mass. It accounts for about 30% of the symptomatic patients with Meckel’s diverticulum. The patient can present with acute abdominal pain, which can be associated with fever and vomiting. If identified on CT, it is seen as a blind-ended diverticulum in the distal small bowel away from the ileocecal junction, demonstrating wall thickening, increased wall enhancement, and surrounding mesenteric fat stranding with associated inflammatory changes in the adjacent segment of the small bowel (Fig. 14). Meckel’s diverticulum can mimic appendicitis or an appendiceal mucocele (Fig. 15). Careful assessment of axial, coronal, and sagittal CT images helps accurately identify Meckel’s diverticulum or diverticulitis. Meckel’s diverticulitis can be complicated by perforation, leading to localized or generalized pneumoperitoneum and secondary abscess formation (Fig. 14). snippets.text: A biopsy of the duodenum is performed during an upper endoscopy to obtain tissue for pathological examination. Duodenal biopsies are performed either randomly for disease detection or surveillance, or directed to correlate with microscopic pathology of likely or apparent abnormal areas in the duodenum. Of note, select pediatric gastroenterology units can perform lactase assays on the biopsies to assess for this enzyme deficiency. One of the most common reasons for conducting a duodenal biopsy is to diagnose or monitor celiac disease.
